## Summary
Provides a practical email structure students can use to request enrollment from instructors while on a course waitlist.

## Common student scenarios
- Course required for major or graduation
- No alternative sections available
- High position on waitlist but no movement

---

## Step-by-step: How to write a waitlist request email

### 1) Subject line
Example:
- Request for Enrollment Permission – [Course Number & Name]

### 2) Greeting
- Use formal greeting (Professor [Last Name])

### 3) Introduce yourself
Include:
- Full name
- Student ID
- Major or program
- Current academic year

### 4) State your request clearly

ast Name])

### 3) Introduce yourself
Include:
- Full name
- Student ID
- Major or program
- Current academic year

### 4) State your request clearly
Example:
"I am currently on the waitlist for [Course Name] and would like to respectfully request permission to enroll."

### 5) Explain academic reason
Good reasons:
- Required for major or graduation timeline
- Prerequisite for upcoming courses
- Limited course offerings

### 6) Close politely
Thank them for time and consideration.

---

## Sample email template

Subject: Request for Enrollment Permission – ECON UN1011

Dear Professor [Last Name],

My name is [Your Name], and I am a [year] student majoring in [major]. I am currently on the waitlist for your course [Course Name and Number] and am writing to respectfully request permission to enroll.

This course is required for my academic plan, and I have limited alternative options this semester. I would greatly appreciate any consideration.

## Common mistakes to avoid
- Sounding demanding
- Writing extremely long explanations
- Sending multiple follow-up emails quickly

---

## Where to submit permission (if approved)
- Through SSOL or registration system
- Using instructor-provided permission code or approval

---

## School-specific notes

## Summary
Most majors have at least one foundational course that unlocks later courses. This document explains the concept and how to find it for ANY major.

## What is a 'gateway course'
A gateway (foundational) course is an early required course that:
- is listed near the beginning of a major sequence
- is a prerequisite for multiple later courses
- reduces planning risk if taken early

## Step-by-step: find the gateway course for ANY major
1) Go to majors index:
   https://bulletin.columbia.edu/general-studies/majors-concentrations/
2) Open the user’s major page
3) Look for the earliest required sequence:

ex:
   https://bulletin.columbia.edu/general-studies/majors-concentrations/
2) Open the user’s major page
3) Look for the earliest required sequence:
   - "Intro to ___"
   - "Foundations of ___"
   - "Prerequisite for upper-level courses"
4) Confirm by checking at least 2 later courses in the major:
   - Do they list this course (or its sequence) as prerequisite?
5) Recommend it as the first-semester anchor

## Example (CS only — example, not universal)
- Example idea: many students treat an intro programming course as a gateway because later CS courses have prerequisites.
- If user is CS and asks “what should I take first”, you can mention:
  "COMS W1004 is commonly used as an intro gateway (confirm via the CS/major pages)."
- Always also provide the CS major page link:
  https://bulletin.columbia.edu/general-studies/majors-concentrations/computer-science/#text

## Safety rule
Do NOT claim a specific course is required for a major unless the major page explicitly says so.

## Step-by-step (universal)
Step 1) Identify the user’s major + year
- Example: "Economics major, first semester" / "CS major, second year"

Step 2) Give the official major link (must)
- Start here: https://bulletin.columbia.edu/general-studies/majors-concentrations/
- Then click their specific major page and provide that link

Step 3) Extract the 3 buckets from the major page
A) Core required courses
B) Foundations / introductory sequence (if listed)

and provide that link

A) Core required courses
B) Foundations / introductory sequence (if listed)
C) Rules for electives/tracks (if listed)

Step 4) Choose 1 foundational “gateway” course first
- Rule: pick the earliest course in the sequence that unlocks later requirements
- If unclear, label as: "Likely gateway (confirm on major page)"

Step 5) Add 1 prerequisite-support course (if needed)
- Common types: math, stats, writing, language, lab co-req
- Only recommend if it helps satisfy prerequisites or degree requirements

Step 6) Add 1 degree/core requirement (if applicable)
- Use the user’s remaining requirements (if known) or suggest checking degree audit/advising

Step 7) Add 0–1 lighter elective (optional)
- Keep total workload realistic

- Use course listing + prereq checks (see separate prereq doc)
